chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhassin al-Maysami said: I was in the presence of Abu Mansur al-Mutatabbib (the physician), and he said: A man from my companions informed me, saying: I, Ibn Abi al-Awja', and Abdullah ibn al-Muqaffa' were in the Sacred Mosque. Ibn al-Muqaffa' said: Do you see these people? — and he gestured with his hand toward

the place of circumambulation (tawaf). None among them deserves the name of humanity except that seated elder — meaning Abu Abd Allah Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him). As for the rest, they are rabble and beasts. Ibn Abi al-Awja' said to him: How did you grant this name to this elder but not to these others? He said: Because I have seen in him what I did not see in them. Ibn Abi al-Awja' said to him: There is no way around testing what you have said about him, from him. He said, and Ibn al-Muqaffa' said to him: Do not do it, for I fear he will corrupt what is in your possession. He said: That is not your real view — rather you fear your opinion of him will weaken in my eyes after you placed him in the station you described. Ibn al-Muqaffa' said: Since you imagine this of me, then go to him, and guard yourself as much as you can against slipping, and do not let your reins turn toward indulgence lest it deliver you into fetters — and put him to the test, whatever turns out for you or against you. He said: So Ibn Abi al-Awja' arose, while I and Ibn al-Muqaffa' remained seated. When Ibn Abi al-Awja' returned to us he said: Woe to you, O Ibn al-Muqaffa'! This is not a human being! And if there is in the world a spiritual being who takes on a body when he wills, manifestly, and becomes spirit again when he wills, invisibly — then he is this one! He said to him: And how is that? He said: I sat with him. When no one was left with him but me, he addressed me first and said: If the matter is as these say — meaning the people of the circumambulation — and it is as they say, then they are saved and you are ruined. And if the matter is as you say, and it is not as you say, then you and they are equal. I said to him: May God have mercy on you — and what do we say and what do they say? My position and theirs is not but one! He said: How can your position and theirs be the same, when they say they have resurrection, reward, and punishment — and they profess that in the heaven there is a god

that in the heaven there is a god and that it is inhabited — while you claim that the heaven is desolate with no one in it. He said: I seized the opportunity from him and said to him: What prevented Him — if the matter is as they say — from appearing to His creation and calling them to His worship, so that no two among them would disagree? And why did He conceal Himself from them and send messengers to them? Had He dealt with them Himself, it would have been more conducive to faith in Him. He said to me: Woe to you! How did He conceal Himself from you, the One who showed you His power in your very self — your arising into being when you did not exist, your maturity after your childhood, your strength after your weakness, your weakness after your strength, your sickness after your health, your health after your sickness, your contentment after your anger, your anger after your contentment, your sadness after your joy, your joy after your sadness, your love after your hatred, your hatred after your love, your resolve after your patience, your patience after your resolve, your desire after your aversion, your aversion after your desire, your inclination after your fear, your fear after your inclination, your hope after your despair, your despair after your hope, your sudden thought about what was not previously in your imagination, and the fading from your mind of what you firmly believed — he continued to enumerate to me His power that is within me, which I could not deny, until I thought he was about to manifest between me and him. Then from one of our companions who reported it with a raised chain (marfu'), and he added to the account of Ibn Abi al-Awja' when Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) questioned him: Ibn Abi al-Awja' returned on the second day to the gathering of Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) and

the second day to the gathering of Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him), and he sat in silence, not speaking. Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said: It seems as if you have come to resume part of what we were discussing. He said: That was my intention, O son of the Messenger of God. Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said to him: How strange is this! You deny God yet you bear witness that I am the son of the Messenger of God. He said: Habit compels me to that. The Scholar (peace be upon him) said to him: And what prevents you from speaking? He said: Out of reverence for you and awe — my tongue does not move freely before you. For I have met scholars and debated theologians, and never has awe come over me the way your awe has come over me. He said: Let that be — but I will open upon you with a question. And he turned toward him and said to him: Are you created or not created? Abd al-Karim ibn Abi al-Awja' said: Rather, I am not created. The Scholar (peace be upon him) said to him: Describe to me — if you were created, how would you be? Abd al-Karim remained for a long while unable to give an answer, and he toyed with a wooden stick that was before him saying: Long, wide, deep, short, moving, still — all of these are the attributes of a created thing. The Scholar said to him: If you know no attribute of creation other than these, then regard yourself as created, because of what you find in yourself of what occurs from these very matters. Abd al-Karim said to him: You have asked me a question that no one has asked me before you, and no one will ask me anything like it after you.

Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said: Suppose you knew that you had not been asked about this in the past — what then tells you that you will not be asked about it in the future? Moreover, O Abd al-Karim, you have contradicted your own claim, because you assert that all things are equal from the very beginning — so how then did you put some first and others last? Then he said: O Abd al-Karim, let me give you further clarity. Consider: if you had a bag filled with jewels, and someone said to you, 'Is there a dinar in the bag?' — and you denied the dinar was in the bag — then he said to you, 'Describe the dinar for me,' but you had no knowledge of what a dinar looks like — would it have been valid for you to deny the existence of a dinar in the bag when you had no knowledge of it? He said: No. So Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said: The universe is greater, longer and wider than the bag — perhaps there is a design within it from which you could not distinguish craftsmanship from its absence. Abd al-Karim was silenced, and some of his companions accepted Islam, while others remained with him. Then he returned on the third day and said: I will reverse the question. Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him) said to him: Ask whatever you wish. He said: What is the proof of the originated nature of bodies? He replied: I have never found anything, small or large, but that when its equal is joined to it, it becomes greater — and in that there is a ceasing and a transition from its first state. And if it were eternal, it would not have ceased nor changed state, because that which ceases and changes state may possibly come into existence and pass out of existence, so its coming into existence

after its non-existence constitutes an entry into origination, and its being in pre-eternity would constitute an entry into non-existence; and never can the attributes of pre-eternity and non-existence and origination and antiquity combine in a single thing. Then Abd al-Karim said: Suppose you have established this by the running of the two states and two times as you mentioned, and derived evidence from that for their origination — but if things remained at their smallness, how would you have been able to prove their origination? The Scholar (peace be upon him) said: We speak only of this world as it exists. If we removed it and placed another world in its place, there would be nothing more indicative of origination than our removing it and placing something else in its stead. But let me answer you from where you supposed you could corner us, and say: if things remained at their smallness, it would still exist within the mind that whenever something is joined to its equal it would become greater — and in the permissibility of change upon it lies its exit from pre-eternity, just as in its actual changing lies its entry into origination. There is nothing beyond this for you, O Abd al-Karim. And he was silenced and humiliated. Then when the following year came, he met him in the Haram. Some of his Shia followers said to him: Ibn Abi al-Awja' has accepted Islam. The Scholar (peace be upon him) said: He is too blind for that — he will not embrace Islam. When he caught sight of the Scholar he said: My master and my guardian! The Scholar (peace be upon him) said to him: What brought you to this place? He replied: The habit of the body and the custom of the city — and to observe what madness the people are engaged in, with the shaving of heads and

the throwing of stones. The Scholar (peace be upon him) said to him: You are still upon your obstinacy and misguidance, O Abd al-Karim. He then proceeded to speak, so the Scholar (peace be upon him) said to him: There is no disputation during the Hajj. And he shook off his cloak from his hand and said: If the matter is as you say — though it is not as you say — we are saved and you are saved too. And if the matter is as we say — and it is as we say — we are saved and you are ruined. Abd al-Karim then turned to those who were with him and said: I felt a stabbing pain in my heart — take me back. So they took him back, and he died. May Allah not have mercy upon him.

key_terms.الدِّينَارُ: The gold coin — used as an analogy to illustrate one cannot deny what one cannot define
key_terms.الرَّعَاعُ: Rabble, commoners, the uneducated masses — used here as a term of contempt
key_terms.الطَّوَاف: The circumambulation of the Ka'ba during Hajj and Umra
key_terms.الْأَزَلُ: Beginningless eternity — the state of having existed from all time
key_terms.الْجِدَالُ فِي الْحَجِّ: Disputation during Hajj — forbidden according to Quran 2:197; the Imam invokes this to cut off debate
key_terms.الْحَدَثُ: Origination, coming into being — the theological term for createdness (opposite of qidam/eternity)
key_terms.الْقِدَمُ: Eternity / pre-eternality — the attribute of having no beginning
key_terms.الْمُتَطَبِّبُ: The physician / one who practices medicine — used as an epithet for Abu Mansur
key_terms.رُوحَانِيٌّ: A spiritual/ethereal being — Ibn Abi al-Awja' uses this in awe of the Imam
key_terms.مَصْنُوعٌ: Made / crafted / created — the Imam's question 'are you made?' forces Abd al-Karim to define creation

ai.seo_question: What arguments did Imam al-Sadiq use to prove the existence of God to atheist Ibn Abi al-Awja'?
ai.summary: This lengthy narrative records a famous three-day theological debate between Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) and the prominent atheist-materialist Abd al-Karim ibn Abi al-Awja', set in Mecca during Hajj. The Imam systematically dismantles the materialist worldview using arguments from the necessity of the Creator evident in the constant change and contingency within the human body, the absurdity of denying what one cannot define (the bag-and-dinar argument), and the logical proof of the createdness of bodies from their susceptibility to change and combination. The narrative concludes with Abd al-Karim's intellectual defeat and ultimate death in denial, serving as a powerful lesson in rational theology (kalam) and the inescapability of recognizing God through reflection on creation.
